title: Rockets: from the soda-bottle rocket to orbit
description: Action and reaction, thrust and impulse, motor classes, stability, drag, parachutes, staging, the Tsiolkovsky equation and orbits — designing and launching rockets in a flight simulator.

rkt-01-garrafa-pet.title: Action and reaction: the soda-bottle rocket
rkt-01-garrafa-pet.theory:
# Every rocket works the same way

A rocket **pushes mass backwards** and, in return, is pushed forwards. This is **Newton's third law**: "for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction".

In the soda-bottle rocket the "pushed mass" is the **water**. The compressed air inside the bottle pushes the water out of the nozzle (the neck) downwards; the water pushes the bottle upwards. It is not the water "hitting the ground" that makes the rocket rise — in space, with no ground at all, a rocket works the same way.

## Momentum

The reaction force (the **thrust**) depends on **how much mass** leaves per second and **how fast** it leaves:

```
thrust = (mass expelled per second) × (exit velocity)
F = ṁ × v
```

Expelling 0.5 kg of water at 20 m/s in 0.1 s gives: F = (0.5 / 0.1) × 20 = 100 N — the weight of a 10 kg object!

## Why water and not just air?

Air is light: even leaving fast, it carries little **momentum**. Water is ~800 times denser, so it carries much more "push". But too much water also hurts: it is heavy, and little air is left to push it (the air loses pressure as it expands). There is an **ideal amount of water**, around **1/3 of the bottle's volume**.

## Pressure

**Pressure** is force per area: 1 bar = 100 000 Pa = 100 000 N/m², roughly the pressure of the atmosphere at sea level. A bicycle pump shows **gauge** pressure (above the atmosphere). On a 22 mm nozzle, each bar of pressure pushes the water with about 76 N — which is why the rocket takes off with accelerations of tens of g.

## The simulator model

- 2 L bottle, 22 mm nozzle, empty bottle + fins + nose = 150 g, plus 40 g of modelling clay in the nose (so the rocket flies straight — we will see why in the stability lesson).
- The air expands without exchanging heat (adiabatic expansion: P × V^1.4 = constant).
- The water speed at the nozzle comes from Bernoulli: v = √(2 × ΔP / ρ). Thrust = 2 × nozzle area × ΔP.
- The final pulse of air (after the water is gone) is ignored; the flight is vertical, with no wind, with air drag.
rkt-01-garrafa-pet.task: Your bottle rocket only climbs about 6 metres. Adjust the **pressure** (6 bar at most — the bottle has a limit!) and the **amount of water** to pass **35 metres** of apogee. Try different amounts of water at the same pressure: there is an ideal point.
rkt-01-garrafa-pet.safety:
- Use **only fizzy-drink PET bottles** (they are made to withstand pressure). **Never** use glass, metal or still-water bottles.
- **Do not go above 5 to 6 bar** and discard bottles that are scratched, dented, old or have been left in the sun.
- Use a **launch base with a remote trigger** (a string several metres long). Nobody leans over the pressurised bottle.
- **Safety glasses** for whoever pumps and launches; everyone **at least 10 m** away and out of the flight line.
- Launch in an **open field**, away from people, animals, cars, trees and power lines, and never towards anyone.
hints: More pressure = more thrust, but the bottle has a limit. Start by testing 4 to 5 bar.
With little water the thrust ends quickly; with too much water the rocket gets heavy and the air loses strength. Try something between 0.5 and 0.7 L.

questions.prompt: Why does the bottle rocket rise?
options: Because the water hits the ground and pushes it
Because the bottle pushes the water down and the water pushes the bottle up
Because the hot air inside the bottle is lighter than the air outside
Because the air pressure pulls the bottle upwards
questions.explanation: Action and reaction (Newton's 3rd law): the force pushing the water down has an equal partner pushing the bottle up. It works even in a vacuum.

questions.prompt: A rocket expels **0.6 kg** of water at **25 m/s** in **0.08 s**. What is the average thrust?
Why use water instead of just compressed air?
options: Water is denser: it expels much more mass and gives much more thrust
Water makes the bottle lighter
Water cools the air and increases the pressure
Only for safety; the thrust is the same
questions.explanation: Thrust is mass per second × velocity. Water has ~800× the density of air, so it carries much more momentum.

rkt-02-empuxo-impulso.title: Thrust, impulse and the rocket motor
rkt-02-empuxo-impulso.theory:
# The motor of a model rocket

A model rocket motor is a cardboard tube with **solid propellant** (black powder or composite), a ceramic **nozzle**, a **delay charge** and an **ejection charge** that opens the parachute. It comes ready-made and certified: you only fit it in and connect the electric igniter.

## Thrust

**Thrust** is the force the motor makes, in **newtons (N)**. It changes during the burn: black-powder motors give a **peak** right at ignition (to get the rocket off the pad) and then hold a lower **plateau**. This graph is the **thrust curve**.

## Total impulse

What really tells "how much the motor pushes" is the **total impulse**:

```
impulse (N·s) = average thrust (N) × burn time (s)
```

It is the **area under the thrust curve**. A 5 N motor for 2 s and a 10 N motor for 1 s have the same impulse: 10 N·s.

By the impulse theorem, impulse = change in momentum (m × Δv). More impulse, more speed — and more height.

## The code printed on the motor

A **C6-5** motor means:

- **C** — the total impulse class (5 to 10 N·s);
- **6** — average thrust of 6 N;
- **5** — 5 seconds of delay between the end of the burn and the parachute ejection.

## The simulator model

The catalogue motors use approximate manufacturer values (impulse, burn time, peak, propellant mass). The curve is a peak followed by a plateau, tuned to give exactly the catalogue impulse. The propellant is consumed in proportion to the impulse already delivered.
rkt-02-empuxo-impulso.task: Your club only allows flights that stay **between 300 and 450 m** high (the field's ceiling). With the B6 the rocket climbs too little. Choose a motor that takes the same rocket into that range.
rkt-02-empuxo-impulso.safety:
- Use **only certified commercial motors** and **never** make, open, modify or "reload" motors or propellant at home — that is how serious burns and explosions happen.
- Follow a **model rocketry safety code** (such as NAR/Tripoli or a local club's) and the **laws of your region**; larger motors usually require certification and authorisation.
- **Electric** ignition, with a removable **safety key** and a countdown said out loud. Minimum distance of **5 m** for small motors (A–D) and more for larger ones.
- Open field, no strong wind, away from buildings, wires and dry brush. Never try to retrieve a rocket stuck in a tree or on a wire.
hints: Each letter has up to double the impulse of the previous one. Go up one letter and see the apogee.
Motors that are too big go past the field's ceiling — and that is forbidden.

questions.prompt: A motor makes an average thrust of **4.5 N** for **1.1 s**. What is the total impulse?
questions.explanation: Impulse = 4.5 N × 1.1 s = 4.95 N·s (a class B motor).

questions.prompt: In the code **D12-5**, what does the **5** mean?
options: 5 N of average thrust
5 seconds of burn
5 seconds of delay between the end of the burn and the parachute ejection
Impulse class 5
questions.explanation: Letter = impulse class, first number = average thrust (N), last number = delay until ejection (s).

questions.prompt: Two motors: one makes 5 N for 2 s; the other makes 10 N for 1 s. What can you say?
options: The 10 N one takes the rocket twice as high
Both have the same total impulse (10 N·s)
The 2 s one has double the impulse
They cannot be compared
questions.explanation: Impulse = thrust × time: 5 × 2 = 10 × 1 = 10 N·s. The apogee may still vary a little (drag, weight), but the "total push" is the same.

rkt-03-classes-empuxo-peso.title: Motor classes and the thrust-to-weight ratio
rkt-03-classes-empuxo-peso.theory:
# Each letter doubles

The total impulse classes follow a scale in which **each letter has up to double the previous one**:

- **A**: up to 2.5 N·s
- **B**: up to 5 N·s
- **C**: up to 10 N·s
- **D**: up to 20 N·s
- **E**: up to 40 N·s
- **F**: up to 80 N·s
- **G**: up to 160 N·s

Up to class G (inclusive) is usually "model rocketry"; from H onwards it is **high-power rocketry**, which requires certification.

## Thrust-to-weight: leaving the pad with force

The **thrust-to-weight ratio** (T/W) compares the average thrust with the weight of the ready rocket (with motor):

```
T/W = average thrust / (mass × 9.81)
```

- T/W < 1: the rocket **does not even leave the ground**.
- T/W between 1 and 5: it leaves slowly; at the end of the rod it is still slow and the wind bends its path.
- **T/W ≥ 5** is the rule of thumb for a straight, safe flight.

That is why each motor has a **maximum lift-off mass**: maximum mass = average thrust / (5 × 9.81).

## Mass: the silent enemy

A lighter rocket accelerates more with the same thrust (a = F/m). But too light is not ideal either: with little inertia, drag slows it down right after the burn. For small rockets, however, **removing weight** almost always helps.
rkt-03-classes-empuxo-peso.task: Your rocket has **150 g** without a motor and the C6 barely lifts it off the ground. Choose the motor and, if needed, reduce the mass to get **thrust/weight ≥ 5** and an apogee **between 300 and 600 m**.
rkt-03-classes-empuxo-peso.safety:
- Respect the **maximum lift-off mass** given by each motor's manufacturer.
- A rocket too heavy for its motor leaves the pad **slowly and crooked** and may fly towards the audience. When in doubt, use a larger **certified** motor or make the rocket lighter — never "boost" a motor.
- Use a **launch rod or rail** long enough for the rocket to gain speed before it is released.
hints: See the thrust/weight in the text below the graph: it changes the moment you change the motor or the mass.
A D12 has an average thrust of ~10 N. With it, how much can the rocket weigh to have T/W ≥ 5?

questions.prompt: What is the **maximum total impulse** of a class **E** motor?
questions.explanation: A = 2.5; B = 5; C = 10; D = 20; E = 40 N·s. Each letter doubles.

questions.prompt: A motor has an average thrust of **10 N**. By the T/W ≥ 5 rule, what is the **maximum lift-off mass** of the rocket (with motor)?
questions.explanation: Maximum weight = 10 / 5 = 2 N. Mass = 2 / 9.81 = 0.2039 kg ≈ 204 g.

questions.prompt: What happens to a rocket with T/W = 1.5?
options: It climbs fast and straight
It does not even leave the pad
It leaves slowly; at the end of the rod it is slow and the wind may deflect it
It explodes
questions.explanation: With a low T/W the acceleration is small (a = (T − W)/m), the rocket leaves the rod slowly and the fins cannot yet keep it straight.

rkt-04-estabilidade.title: Stability: the CG ahead of the CP
rkt-04-estabilidade.theory:
# Two centres that decide everything

- **Centre of gravity (CG)**: the point where the rocket balances on your finger. It is where the weight "acts".
- **Centre of pressure (CP)**: the point where the air forces "act" when the rocket tilts a little.

If the rocket tilts in flight, the air hits it from the side. If the **CP is behind the CG**, that force pushes the **tail** back into the line of flight: the rocket straightens itself, like an arrow or a weathervane. If the CP is **ahead of** the CG, the force increases the tilt: the rocket **tumbles**.

## The stability margin

```
margin (calibres) = (CP position − CG position) / diameter
```

(positions measured from the tip of the nose)

- **below 0**: unstable — dangerous;
- **0 to 1**: barely stable, it wobbles;
- **1 to 2**: the ideal for most rockets;
- **above 3**: too stable — it turns into the wind ("weathercocking") and flies crooked on windy days.

## How to move the CP and the CG

- **Larger fins** move the CP **backwards** (more area at the back).
- **Weight in the nose** (modelling clay) moves the CG **forwards**.
- **A longer rocket** moves the fins away from the nose: the CP moves backwards.
- A heavy motor in the tail moves the CG backwards: a rocket that is stable with a small motor can become unstable with a big one.

## The Barrowman method (simplified)

The simulator computes the CP with the **Barrowman method** (1966), still used by programs like OpenRocket: it adds the "force" of the nose (always 2, at a point that depends on its shape) and that of the fins (which grows with the square of the span divided by the diameter), and finds the weighted mean point. The body tube does not count at small angles. The CG takes into account the body (centre in the middle), the motor (in the tail) and the nose weight.

In the simulated flight, a rocket with a negative margin tumbles: it loses almost all useful thrust and the drag triples.
rkt-04-estabilidade.task: This rocket has tiny fins and **tumbles**. Get the **stability margin between 1 and 2.5 calibres** and make it climb at least **150 m** with the B6 motor. Watch the CG (blue) and the CP (red) in the drawing of the rocket.
rkt-04-estabilidade.safety:
- **Never launch an unstable rocket.** It tumbles and may fly in any direction, including towards the audience.
- Before flying, do the **string test**: tie the rocket (with motor) at the balance point (CG) and swing it in circles. If it flies nose first, it is stable.
hints: Increase the fin span and watch the CP (red dot) move backwards.
Weight in the nose also helps, but makes the rocket heavier (less height).

questions.prompt: For a rocket to be stable, where must the CG be?
options: Behind the CP (closer to the tail)
Ahead of the CP (closer to the nose)
Exactly at the CP
It does not matter, what matters is the motor
questions.explanation: With the CG ahead of the CP, any tilt creates an air force that pushes the tail back: the rocket straightens itself.

questions.prompt: A rocket with a diameter of **25 mm** has its CP at **320 mm** and its CG at **270 mm** from the tip. What is the stability margin, in calibres?
What happens when you put modelling clay inside the nose?
options: The CP moves forwards and stability drops
The CG moves forwards and stability increases
The CG moves backwards and stability increases
Nothing changes in the stability
questions.explanation: Weight at the front pulls the CG towards the nose, increasing the distance to the CP. In return, the rocket gets heavier.

rkt-05-arrasto.title: Aerodynamics: drag and the shape of the nose
rkt-05-arrasto.theory:
# The force of the air

Air slows down everything that moves through it. This force is **drag**:

```
F_drag = ½ × ρ × v² × Cd × A
```

- **ρ** (rho): air density — 1.225 kg/m³ at sea level, halving at about 6 km of altitude;
- **v**: speed — it enters **squared**: double the speed gives **4×** the drag;
- **A**: frontal area (π × d² / 4) — doubling the diameter gives **4×** the area;
- **Cd**: drag coefficient — "how aerodynamic" the shape is.

## Where a rocket's Cd comes from

- **Nose**: an ogive or a cone lets the air slide by; a blunt (flat) nose hits the air head-on.
- **Base**: behind the rocket a low-pressure wake forms and "sucks" backwards.
- **Friction**: the air scrapes along the whole surface of the body and fins. The larger the wetted area, the more friction.

Typical model rockets have a Cd between **0.4 and 0.75**.

## Is thinner better?

For the same motor, a **thin** rocket has much less frontal area. But be careful: making it thin also changes the **stability** (the diameter enters the CP and margin calculation). Designing is balancing.

## The simulator model

Cd = nose (ogive 0.10; cone 0.15; rounded 0.25; blunt 0.55) + base 0.12 + friction of the body and fins. The air density drops with altitude (ρ = 1.225 × e^(−h/8500)). Near the speed of sound (340 m/s) the drag grows up to double.
rkt-05-arrasto.task: With a C6, this fat, blunt-nosed rocket only climbs ~160 m. Change the **nose**, the **diameter** and the **fins** to pass **330 m**, keeping the stability margin **≥ 1 calibre**.
hints: An ogive nose has a much lower Cd than a blunt one.
The diameter enters squared in the frontal area. A 25 mm tube has less than half the area of a 41 mm one.
When you make the rocket thinner, check the margin: the fins may need to change.

questions.prompt: Calculate the drag of a rocket at **50 m/s**, with **Cd = 0.5** and a frontal area of **0.0005 m²**, at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³).
If the rocket's speed doubles, the drag…
options: also doubles
becomes 4 times larger
becomes 8 times larger
does not change
questions.explanation: Drag depends on v²: (2v)² = 4v².

questions.prompt: Why does a rocket slow down less up high (at 10 km altitude)?
options: Because gravity disappears
Because the air is less dense: smaller ρ, smaller drag
Because it is colder and the Cd drops
Because the frontal area decreases
questions.explanation: The air density roughly halves every 6 km; at 10 km it is only ~1/3 of the sea-level value.

goals: Stability margin of at least 1 calibre

rkt-06-recuperacao.title: Recovery: parachutes and ejection delay
rkt-06-recuperacao.theory:
# Going up is half the flight

A rocket has to come back in one piece (and without hurting anyone). That is why it has a **recovery system**, almost always a **parachute**.

## The right moment to open

The ideal is to open the parachute **at apogee**, when the speed is almost zero.

- **Too early**: the rocket is still climbing fast; the parachute opens with a huge jerk and may tear or come off.
- **Too late**: the rocket is already falling fast; same jerk — or it hits the ground first.

In model rocket motors, the **delay** is the last number of the code (C6-**5**): the seconds between the **end of the burn** and the **ejection**. The right value is:

```
ideal delay ≈ (time to apogee) − (burn time)
```

## Landing speed

Descending under a parachute, the rocket soon reaches **terminal velocity**: the parachute drag equals the weight.

```
m × g = ½ × ρ × v² × Cd × A   →   v = √( 2 × m × g / (ρ × Cd × A) )
```

With a round parachute (Cd ≈ 0.8), we want to land at **3.5 to 5 m/s** — like jumping from a height of 60 cm to 1.3 m. Faster breaks fins; slower and the wind carries the rocket far away.

## The simulator model

The parachute opens at the instant "end of burn + delay" and inflates in 0.4 s. Parachute Cd = 0.8 over the area of the circle.
rkt-06-recuperacao.task: This rocket's parachute opens at over 70 m/s (it would tear!) and is too small. Choose the **parachute diameter** and the **ejection delay** so that it opens at **15 m/s at most** and the rocket lands at **5 m/s at most**.
rkt-06-recuperacao.safety:
- Use **fire-resistant wadding** between the motor and the parachute: the ejection charge is hot and melts nylon.
- If the parachute does not open, the rocket falls like an arrow: **stay alert and shout "heads up!"** — that is why everyone stands back and watches the flight.
- Never try to recover a rocket from **power lines**, high roofs or tall trees.
hints: Run once and see the apogee time and the burn time in the text. The ideal delay is the difference.
The landing speed drops with the square root of the parachute area: doubling the diameter quadruples the area and halves the speed.

questions.prompt: A **0.1 kg** rocket descends under a parachute with **Cd = 0.8** and an area of **0.1257 m²** (40 cm diameter). What is the terminal velocity at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
The rocket reaches apogee **7.5 s** after ignition and the motor burns for **1.9 s**. What is the best ejection delay?
questions.explanation: 7.5 − 1.9 = 5.6 s. In practice we choose the motor with the closest delay (C6-5 or C6-7).

questions.prompt: Why **not** open the parachute right at the end of the burn?
options: Because the motor is still hot
Because the rocket is still fast: the jerk may tear the parachute
Because the parachute would make the rocket climb higher
There is no problem at all
questions.explanation: At the end of the burn the rocket is near its maximum speed; the opening force grows with v².

goals: Parachute opens at 15 m/s at most

rkt-07-estagios.title: Multi-stage rockets
rkt-07-estagios.theory:
# Why throw part of the rocket away?

When a rocket's motor runs out, the empty tube, the fins and the spent motor are still there — **dead mass** that the rest of the flight has to carry. The idea of the **stage** is: when a motor runs out, we **drop the part that became useless** and light the next motor on a lighter rocket.

## How it works in a model rocket

- The **lower stage** (booster) uses a **zero-delay** motor (e.g. B6-**0**).
- When it finishes, its ejection charge — instead of opening a parachute — **ignites the upper motor** and pushes the booster away.
- The **upper stage** (sustainer) continues with its normal motor (e.g. C6-7), already moving and lighter.

## Why does it go higher than just adding the motors?

The upper motor starts burning **already at high speed**, at a greater height and **without carrying the booster**. Each newton-second of the second motor yields more.

In real rockets (space launchers) stages are even more important: a single stage that reached orbit would have to be almost all tank — we will see why with the Tsiolkovsky equation.

## The simulator model

The second motor ignites the instant the first one ends. The dropped booster (structure + spent motor) stops counting. The stability shown is that of the upper stage (the booster has its own fins).
rkt-07-estagios.task: The competition rules allow **15 N·s of total impulse at most**, and the goal is to pass **480 m**. A single C6 does not get there. Build a **2-stage** rocket that wins.
rkt-07-estagios.safety:
- Multi-stage rockets are for those who have mastered single-stage ones: the lower stage falls **without a parachute** (it must be light, with large fins, to fall "gliding" slowly) and the upper one climbs much higher.
- Use only motors made for the lower stage (**zero** delay, such as the B6-0) and check the clear area — it needs to be larger.
hints: Switch to 2 stages and combine motors: the total impulse is the sum of the two.
B6 (5 N·s) + C6 (10 N·s) = 15 N·s, within the rules.

questions.prompt: A booster with **B6-0** (5 N·s) and a sustainer with **C6-7** (10 N·s). What is the rocket's total impulse?
questions.explanation: The impulses add up: 5 + 10 = 15 N·s.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a multi-stage rocket?
options: Motors get more powerful when stacked
You drop the mass that is no longer useful (spent motor, tube, fins), and the rest accelerates more
The rocket becomes more stable
The drag disappears
questions.explanation: Less dead mass = more acceleration with the same thrust, and the 2nd motor already starts fast and high.

questions.prompt: Why must the lower stage's motor have **zero** delay?
options: To ignite the upper motor as soon as it ends, without losing speed
To open the booster's parachute
To save propellant
Because it is cheaper
questions.explanation: Any wait would make the rocket lose speed (gravity and drag) before the 2nd motor ignites.

goals: Total impulse of at most 15 N·s

rkt-08-tsiolkovsky.title: The Tsiolkovsky equation and delta-v
rkt-08-tsiolkovsky.theory:
# The rocket equation

In 1903, the Russian teacher **Konstantin Tsiolkovsky** wrote the equation that rules all of astronautics:

```
Δv = ve × ln( m0 / mf )
```

- **Δv** (delta-v): how much the rocket can change its speed, if there were no gravity or air;
- **ve**: exhaust gas velocity (ve = Isp × g0, with g0 = 9.81 m/s²);
- **m0**: initial mass (full); **mf**: final mass (without propellant);
- **ln**: natural logarithm (the "ln" key on the calculator).

## Isp: the motor's "efficiency"

The **specific impulse** (Isp, in seconds) says how much impulse each kilogram of propellant gives: Isp = impulse / (propellant mass × g0).

- black powder (model rocket): ~80 s
- composite solid propellant: 200–270 s
- kerosene + liquid oxygen: 300–350 s
- hydrogen + liquid oxygen: ~450 s

## The tyranny of the logarithm

Because Δv grows with the **logarithm** of the mass ratio, doubling the propellant does **not** double the Δv. To always gain the same 2 900 m/s with Isp 300 s, the mass ratio has to **multiply** by e (2.72) each time. That is why rockets are almost all tank — and why stages are used.

## Real vs ideal delta-v

The real flight loses Δv to **gravity** (each second climbing vertically costs 9.81 m/s) and to **drag**. Motors that burn too slowly lose more to gravity; those that burn too fast suffer huge accelerations.

## The simulator model

In the "custom" motor, thrust = Isp × g0 × mass flow rate, constant until the propellant runs out. The simulator shows the ideal Δv (Tsiolkovsky) and flies the rocket for real, with gravity that decreases with altitude and a thinning atmosphere: compare the two!
rkt-08-tsiolkovsky.task: This sounding rocket (60 kg without propellant) only has an ideal Δv of ~1.9 km/s and climbs 17 km. Adjust **Isp**, **propellant mass**, **flow rate** and **dry mass** to get **ideal Δv ≥ 3 000 m/s** and pass **80 km** of apogee.
hints: A better composite propellant (Isp 250 s) already helps a lot: Δv is proportional to Isp.
More propellant increases m0/mf — but remember the logarithm. More flow rate shortens the burn and reduces gravity losses.

questions.prompt: A rocket with **Isp = 300 s** has an initial mass of **100 t** and a final mass of **25 t**. What is the ideal Δv? (g0 = 9.81 m/s²)
A C6 motor delivers **10 N·s** burning **12.3 g** of black powder. What is the approximate Isp?
questions.explanation: Isp = 10 / (0.0123 × 9.81) ≈ 82.9 s — typical of black powder.

questions.prompt: If you **double** the mass ratio m0/mf, the Δv…
options: doubles
increases by ve × ln 2 (≈ 0.69 × ve), no matter what it started from
quadruples
does not change
questions.explanation: ln(2R) = ln R + ln 2: each doubling adds the same fixed amount to Δv. That is why getting to space is so hard.

goals: Ideal Δv of at least 3 000 m/s

rkt-09-orbita.title: Orbit: orbital velocity and the Hohmann transfer
rkt-09-orbita.theory:
# Being in orbit is falling without ever arriving

Imagine a cannon on top of a mountain (the idea is Newton's own). The faster the ball leaves, the farther it falls. At a certain speed, the Earth "curves" away beneath the ball as fast as it falls: the ball **never reaches the ground**. That is an **orbit**.

## Orbital velocity

In a circular orbit, gravity plays the role of the centripetal force:

```
v = √( G × M / r )
```

- G × M (Earth) = 3.986 × 10^14 m³/s²
- r = Earth's radius (6 371 km) + altitude

At 400 km (the Space Station) this gives ~7.7 km/s: one lap around the Earth every 92 minutes. **Going high is easy; going fast sideways is what is hard.** A sounding rocket climbs 100 km, but falls back because it has no horizontal speed.

## The Δv budget to orbit

To reach a low orbit a launcher needs **~9.4 km/s** of Δv: ~7.8 km/s of orbital velocity + ~1.5–2 km/s lost to gravity, drag and manoeuvres. With an Isp of 300–450 s, Tsiolkovsky demands mass ratios of 10 to 20 — impossible with a single stage and a real structure. That is why launchers have **2 or 3 stages**.

## Thrust-to-weight at lift-off

First of all, the rocket has to **leave the ground**: T/W > 1 (in practice 1.2 to 1.5). Large launchers do not use fins: they swivel the engine (**thrust vectoring**) to stay pointed.

## Hohmann transfer

To go from a low circular orbit to a higher one (for example, a geostationary satellite), the most economical way is the **Hohmann transfer** (1925):

- **1st burn**: accelerate **forwards** in the low orbit. The orbit becomes an **ellipse** whose highest point (apogee) touches the desired orbit.
- Half a lap later, at apogee, the spacecraft is **slower** than needed for the circular orbit there.
- **2nd burn**: accelerate again **forwards** at apogee, and the orbit becomes circular.

Curiously: the higher orbit is **slower**, even though you accelerated twice — the energy went into height.

## The simulator model

Here the simulator flies **vertically** (it does not enter orbit): use it for the mass, Isp and thrust budget. Δv is the ideal Tsiolkovsky value summed over the two stages; the launcher is guided by thrust vectoring.
rkt-09-orbita.task: A 2-stage launcher takes 1 t to space. Right now it **does not even leave the ground** (thrust/weight < 1) and has a Δv of only ~8.9 km/s. Adjust the 1st stage's **Isp** and **flow rate** and the 2nd stage's **Isp** and **propellant** to get **T/W ≥ 1.2** and **Δv ≥ 9 400 m/s**.
hints: Thrust = Isp × 9.81 × flow rate. With ~50 t the rocket weighs ~490 kN; for T/W ≥ 1.2 the 1st stage needs about 600 kN (more, if you put more propellant on top).
In the upper stage Isp is worth gold: vacuum engines reach 340–450 s. More propellant in the 2nd stage also helps a lot.

questions.prompt: What is the speed of a circular orbit at **400 km** altitude? Use G·M = 3.986 × 10^14 m³/s² and an Earth radius of 6 371 km.
In a Hohmann transfer to a **higher** orbit, the two burns are…
options: backwards (braking), so the spacecraft "falls upwards"
forwards in both: at the low point of the ellipse and then at the high point
upwards (in the radial direction), pointing away from the Earth
one forwards and the other backwards
questions.explanation: The 1st burn (prograde) creates the transfer ellipse; the 2nd, at apogee, circularises the orbit.

questions.prompt: If low orbit asks for ~7.8 km/s, why does the launcher need ~9.4 km/s of Δv?
options: Because the fuel evaporates
Because of the losses to gravity and drag during the climb
Because the Earth rotates the wrong way
The engineers' safety margin
questions.explanation: While climbing, the rocket spends thrust just to avoid falling (gravity loss) and to overcome the air (drag loss).

goals: Ideal Δv of at least 9 400 m/s (low orbit)

rkt-10-missao-sondagem.title: Full project: sounding mission to space
rkt-10-missao-sondagem.theory:
# From the blank page to the mission

Real engineering means meeting **several requirements at the same time**. A university team has to take a 10 kg scientific payload (the rocket weighs 60 kg without propellant) beyond the **Kármán line (100 km)**, where we conventionally say space begins, and bring it back in one piece.

## The mission requirements

- **Apogee ≥ 100 km**.
- **Maximum acceleration ≤ 15 g** — the payload and the electronics have a limit.
- **Stability margin between 1.5 and 4 calibres** — the rocket climbs through dense air at over 1 km/s.
- **Parachute opening at ≤ 50 m/s** and **landing at ≤ 10 m/s**.

## The design budget

Start with the **Δv**. Without air and with constant gravity, reaching a height h would require v = √(2 × g × h) ≈ 1.4 km/s for 100 km. Adding the losses to gravity during the burn and to drag, we need **~3 km/s or more**.

Then the **acceleration**: the peak is at the end of the burn, when the rocket is lightest (a = F/m_final − g). More mass flow = shorter burn, less gravity loss — but more g's. Balancing this is the art.

Finally, **stability** (fins compatible with the CG full of propellant) and **recovery** (a parachute big enough and a delay that opens it near apogee).

## Mind the delay

In a flight of almost 4 minutes to apogee, the ejection delay is not a matter of seconds: it is the difference between the apogee time and the end of the burn. In the simulator, the parachute opens at that instant and the rocket descends with it open (the model does not compute the heating or loads of re-entry).

## Design cycle

1. Estimate (Δv, T/W, accelerations).
2. Simulate.
3. See which requirement failed and why.
4. Change **one thing at a time** and simulate again.
rkt-10-missao-sondagem.task: Design the mission: adjust **propellant**, **flow rate**, **Isp**, **fins**, **parachute** and **delay** to meet **all** the requirements. Engineer's tip: first reach 100 km with ≤ 15 g; then get the stability right; recovery last.
rkt-10-missao-sondagem.safety: Rockets like this are projects of **universities, agencies and licensed teams**, with controlled launch areas (such as the Barreira do Inferno or Alcântara Launch Centres) and authorisation from the aviation authorities. Here it is **simulation only**: never try to build motors or propellants.
hints: With Isp 250 s and ~170 kg of propellant the Δv exceeds 3.2 km/s. A flow rate of ~3 kg/s keeps the acceleration below 15 g.
Run it, note the apogee time and the end of the burn, and use the difference as the delay.
A parachute of ~5 m diameter holds 60 kg at under 10 m/s.

questions.prompt: A flight reaches apogee **218 s** after ignition and the burn ends at **57 s**. What delay makes the parachute open at apogee?
What mass ratio m0/mf does a rocket with **Isp 250 s** need for **Δv = 3 300 m/s**?
Why does the maximum acceleration happen at the **end** of the burn, and not at the start?
options: Because the thrust increases with altitude
Because the rocket is lighter: with the same thrust, a = F/m grows
Because the drag pushes the rocket upwards
Because gravity disappears in space
questions.explanation: With constant thrust, the mass drops as the propellant burns; at the end only ~60 kg remain for the same thrust.

goals: Apogee of at least 100 km (Kármán line)
Parachute opens at 50 m/s at most

rkt-11-agua-otima.title: Water rocket: a bigger bottle and the sweet spot
rkt-11-agua-otima.theory:
# The energy is in the air, the mass is in the water

In a water rocket, the **compressed air stores the energy** and the **water is the mass thrown backwards**. Both compete for the same space inside the bottle:

- **Too little water**: plenty of air, but the water runs out in hundredths of a second and the rocket gets little "push".
- **Too much water**: the air expands only a little before the pressure drops, and the rocket still carries heavy water that has barely left.

The sweet spot is near **1/3 of the volume** — and it changes with the bottle size, the pressure and the nozzle.

## Thrust and exit velocity

With gauge pressure ΔP at a nozzle of area A:

```
water velocity  v = √(2 × ΔP / ρ)
thrust          F = 2 × A × ΔP
```

With 5 bar on a 22 mm nozzle: v ≈ 31.6 m/s and F ≈ 380 N — over 100 g of acceleration on a light rocket!

## Why the bigger bottle goes higher

The energy stored in the air grows with **pressure × volume**. A 3 L bottle at the same pressure stores 50% more energy, and the air loses pressure more slowly while it pushes the water. The peak acceleration, however, comes at the **end** of the burn, when the bottle is light — so you must also look after the **payload** (an egg, a camera) in the nose.

## In this lab

The bottle is now **3 L** (same 22 mm nozzle). The empty mass, the nose and the fins are the same as in lesson 1.
rkt-11-agua-otima.task: With the **3 L** bottle, go above **60 m** of apogee without the peak acceleration exceeding **100 g** (the camera in the nose can't take more than that). Adjust the **pressure** and the **water**.
rkt-11-agua-otima.safety:
- **3 L** bottles store more energy: the same rules apply even more strictly — only fizzy-drink PET, **6 bar at most**, remote trigger and **safety glasses**.
- Never pressurise a spliced bottle (two bottles joined) without a hydrostatic test with water first.
- Everyone **at least 10 m** away, out of the flight line.
hints: Start at 5 bar and test the water in steps of 0.2 L. Write down the apogee and the peak acceleration of each try.
A third of 3 L is 1 L. More water makes the rocket heavier at the end of the burn — and the peak acceleration drops.

questions.prompt: What is the initial thrust of a water rocket with a **22 mm** nozzle at **5 bar** (F = 2 × A × ΔP)?
At **5 bar** gauge pressure, how fast does the water leave the nozzle? (v = √(2 × ΔP / ρ), ρ = 1000 kg/m³)
Why does the peak acceleration **drop** when you add more water (at the same pressure)?
options: Because the water lowers the starting pressure
Because, while the thrust is still strong, there is still a lot of heavy water on board
Because the water makes the nozzle bigger
Because gravity is stronger with more water
questions.explanation: a = F / m. With more water, the air has expanded more and the pressure has already dropped by the time the bottle is light; the peak of F/m is lower.

rkt-12-estavel-demais.title: Overstable: weathercocking and the price of fins
rkt-12-estavel-demais.theory:
# More stability is not always better

In the stability lesson we saw that the **CG must be ahead of the CP**, with a margin of **1 to 2 calibers**. Why not just fit huge fins and lots of nose weight "to be safe"?

## Weathercocking

When the rocket leaves the rod in a crosswind, the air arrives slightly from the side. The fins turn the nose **into the wind**, like a weather vane. The **bigger the margin**, the stronger this correction: a rocket with a 4-caliber margin can turn 20° or 30° into the wind, fly low and land far away.

## The cost of fins and ballast

- **Big fins** add wetted area and skin-friction drag (Cd goes up).
- **Nose weight** is extra mass the motor has to lift.

Both **steal altitude**. A good design has **enough** margin, not the most.

## Calibers

```
margin (calibers) = (CP − CG) / diameter
```

A 30 mm rocket with the CP at 380 mm and the CG at 290 mm from the tip has a margin of 90 / 30 = **3 calibers** — overstable for most flights.

## In this lab

The rocket (25 mm, 400 mm, C6 motor) came from another club with huge fins and 20 g of clay in the nose. Bring the margin back into the good range and win back the altitude.
rkt-12-estavel-demais.task: Bring the stability margin **between 1 and 2 calibers** and make the rocket pass **400 m** of apogee, changing the **fin span** and the **nose weight**.
rkt-12-estavel-demais.safety:
- An **overstable** rocket turns into the wind ("weathercocking") and can fly low and far: **don't launch in winds above ~30 km/h** and tilt the launch rod at most a few degrees **downwind**.
- Keep the landing area clear of people and cars.
hints: Remove the nose weight first: it only costs altitude if the rocket is already stable.
Then shrink the fins little by little and watch the margin: below ~22 mm it drops under 1 caliber.

questions.prompt: A **30 mm** rocket has the CP at **380 mm** and the CG at **290 mm** from the tip. What is the stability margin?
questions.explanation: (380 − 290) / 30 = 3 calibers: overstable, it will weathercock in a crosswind.

questions.prompt: In a crosswind, an overstable rocket…
options: Flies straight, ignoring the wind
Turns downwind
Turns its nose into the wind and flies tilted
Starts tumbling end over end and falls
questions.explanation: The fins line the rocket up with the relative wind, which comes slightly from the side: the nose points into the wind. The bigger the margin, the bigger the turn.

questions.prompt: A **41 mm** diameter rocket should have a **1.5-caliber** margin. How many millimetres ahead of the CP should the CG be?

rkt-13-bocal.title: The nozzle: turning pressure into speed
rkt-13-bocal.theory:
# What the nozzle is for

In the combustion chamber the gases are **hot and at high pressure**, but almost still. The nozzle turns that pressure into **exit velocity**: the faster the gas leaves, the more thrust per kilogram of propellant (the Isp).

## Converging–diverging (de Laval)

A rocket nozzle **narrows** down to the **throat** and then **widens** again:

- In the converging part the gas speeds up to the **speed of sound** exactly at the throat (**choked** flow — the mass flow depends only on the chamber pressure and the throat area).
- In the diverging part, a **supersonic** gas does the opposite of what intuition says: as the tube **widens** it **accelerates** even more, while pressure and temperature drop.

The **expansion ratio** is ε = A_exit / A_throat.

## The full thrust

```
F = ṁ × ve + (pe − pa) × Ae
```

- ṁ: mass flow; ve: exit velocity;
- pe: pressure at the nozzle exit; pa: ambient pressure; Ae: exit area.

The second term is the **pressure thrust**. At sea level (pa ≈ 1 bar), a nozzle that releases the gas at 0.5 bar loses thrust (**over-expanded**); in vacuum (pa = 0) the same nozzle gains thrust. That is why an engine has a lower **sea-level Isp** than its **vacuum Isp**, and upper-stage engines use huge nozzles.

## Ideal design

The ideal nozzle has pe = pa. Since the air pressure drops during the climb, no fixed nozzle is ideal all the time: first-stage nozzles are a compromise; second-stage ones are optimised for vacuum. A nozzle that is too over-expanded on the ground can suffer **flow separation** and vibrate.

questions.prompt: In the **diverging** part of the nozzle (after the throat), the supersonic gas…
options: Slows down, because the tube gets wider
Speeds up, while pressure and temperature drop
Keeps its speed and only cools down
Becomes subsonic again
questions.explanation: In supersonic flow, increasing the area makes the gas accelerate (the opposite of subsonic flow). That is why the nozzle widens after the throat.

questions.prompt: An engine has ṁ = **100 kg/s**, ve = **2500 m/s**, exit pressure **0.5 bar** and exit area **0.5 m²**. What is the thrust at sea level (pa = 101 325 Pa)?
questions.explanation: F = 100 × 2500 + (50 000 − 101 325) × 0.5 = 250 000 − 25 662 ≈ 224 300 N. The nozzle is over-expanded at sea level.

questions.prompt: And the same engine in **vacuum** (pa = 0)?
questions.explanation: F = 250 000 + 50 000 × 0.5 = 275 000 N. With no air outside, the pressure thrust now helps.

questions.prompt: What is this engine's **vacuum Isp**? (Isp = F / (ṁ × g0), g0 = 9.80665 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Isp = 275 000 / (100 × 9.80665) ≈ 280 s. At sea level it would be only ≈ 229 s.

questions.prompt: The throat is **0.2 m** in diameter and the exit **0.8 m**. What is the expansion ratio ε = A_exit / A_throat?
questions.explanation: Area grows with the square of the diameter: (0.8 / 0.2)² = 4² = 16.

rkt-14-propelentes.title: Propellants: solid, liquid and hybrid
rkt-14-propelentes.theory:
# What burns in a rocket

A rocket carries **fuel and oxidiser** (it doesn't use the oxygen in the air). There are three families:

- **Solid**: fuel and oxidiser mixed in one block (the "grain"). Simple, stores for years, lots of thrust — but it **can't be shut down or throttled** once lit. E.g. model rocket motors, strap-on boosters. Typical Isp 250–270 s.
- **Liquid**: two tanks and pumps (or pressurisation). It can be **throttled, shut down and restarted**. E.g. kerosene + liquid oxygen (RP-1/LOX, Isp ~300–340 s), methane/LOX (~330–360 s), hydrogen/LOX (~450 s).
- **Hybrid**: solid fuel (rubber, paraffin) and liquid or gaseous oxidiser. Safer than solid and simpler than liquid; intermediate Isp.

## Mixture ratio O/F

It is the ratio between the mass of **oxidiser** and of **fuel** that flows in each second. RP-1/LOX uses O/F ≈ 2.56: out of every 3.56 kg, 2.56 kg is oxygen.

## Why hydrogen has such a high Isp

The exit velocity grows with the chamber **temperature** and falls with the **molar mass** of the gas:

```
ve ∝ √(T / M)
```

Light gases (water vapour + hydrogen, M ≈ 10–12 g/mol) leave much faster. If M is halved at the same temperature, ve grows √2 ≈ 1.41 times.

## The price: density

Liquid hydrogen has only **71 kg/m³** (RP-1: ~810 kg/m³). Huge tanks = heavy structure and lots of drag. That is why hydrogen shines in **upper stages**, while the first stage prefers **dense** propellants (kerosene, methane, solids) — high thrust from a small tank.

## Safety

Real propellants are **toxic, cryogenic or explosive**: work for licensed professionals in proper facilities only. At home, only certified commercial motors.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of a **solid** propellant motor?
options: It needs complicated pumps
It can't be stored for long
Once lit, it can't be throttled or shut down
It gives little thrust
questions.explanation: The grain burns to the end. That's why solids are great as boosters, but precise orbit insertion is usually left to liquid engines.

questions.prompt: An RP-1/LOX engine burns **100 kg/s** of propellant at O/F = **2.56**. How many kg/s are oxygen?
If the molar mass of the exhaust gases is **halved** and the chamber temperature doesn't change, the exit velocity is multiplied by how much? (ve ∝ √(T/M))
What tank volume do **10 tonnes** of liquid hydrogen (ρ = **71 kg/m³**) take up?
questions.explanation: V = 10 000 / 71 ≈ 140.8 m³. The same mass of RP-1 would fit in ~12.3 m³.

questions.prompt: Why is hydrogen, which has the highest Isp, usually used in **upper stages**?
options: Because it doesn't work at sea level
Because it has low density: huge tanks are heavy and draggy in the air; higher up, the high Isp pays off
Because it is cheaper
Because it produces more thrust per nozzle
questions.explanation: On the first stage what matters is high thrust and compact tanks (dense propellants); in vacuum, every second of Isp is worth a lot of Δv.

rkt-15-estagios-otimos.title: Optimal staging and the structural fraction
rkt-15-estagios-otimos.theory:
# Why split the rocket

By the Tsiolkovsky equation, Δv = ve × ln(m0 / mf). The problem is the **structure**: tanks, engines and skin all weigh something. In a single-stage rocket, that mass rides along to the end, and the mass ratio is limited.

By **dropping** the empty tank, the upper stage starts "from scratch" with a new mass ratio — and the Δv values **add up**:

```
total Δv = Σ ve,i × ln(m0,i / mf,i)
```

## Structural fraction

The **structural coefficient** ε = m_structure / (m_structure + m_propellant) tells how much of the stage is "dead weight". Real rockets have ε ≈ 0.05–0.10. With ε = 0.1 and no payload, the best possible mass ratio of one stage is 1/ε = 10 — and with Isp 300 s that gives at most ~6.8 km/s, less than the ~9.4 km/s needed for orbit. **A single stage can't reach orbit with margin**; two or three can.

## The optimal split

For **identical** stages (same Isp and same ε), the optimal split gives **the same Δv to each stage**. Two stages with mass ratio 3 and Isp 300 s give 2 × 300 × 9.81 × ln 3 ≈ **6.46 km/s**.

## Payload fraction

The payload is usually only **1 to 4%** of the liftoff mass. Each extra stage improves the Δv but adds engines, separations and failure points — the gains shrink after 3 or 4 stages.

## Required mass ratio

Inverting Tsiolkovsky:

```
m0 / mf = e^(Δv / ve)
```

With Isp 350 s (ve ≈ 3432 m/s), for Δv = 4.5 km/s: m0/mf = e^1.311 ≈ 3.71.

questions.prompt: Two stages, each with **Isp = 300 s** and mass ratio **3**. What is the total ideal Δv? (g0 = 9.80665 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Each stage: 300 × 9.80665 × ln 3 ≈ 3232 m/s. Total ≈ 6464 m/s.

questions.prompt: What mass ratio m0/mf does a stage with **Isp = 350 s** need to give **Δv = 4500 m/s**?
A stage has structural coefficient **ε = 0.1** and no payload. What is the largest possible mass ratio m0/mf?
questions.explanation: m0 = structure + propellant; mf = structure. m0/mf = 1/ε = 10.

questions.prompt: For **identical** stages (same Isp and same structural fraction), which split gives the largest total Δv?
options: The same Δv for each stage
Almost all the propellant in the first stage
Almost all the propellant in the last stage
It makes no difference
questions.explanation: It is the classic result of the Lagrange-multiplier optimisation: identical stages should split the Δv equally.

questions.prompt: Why do launchers rarely have more than 3 or 4 stages?
options: Because the law forbids it
Because the Δv gain shrinks and each stage adds cost, mass and failure risk
Because extra stages reduce the Δv
Because the rocket would become unstable
questions.explanation: The extra Δv from each new stage keeps getting smaller, while separations, ignitions and interfaces are costly failure points.

rkt-16-perdas-gravidade.title: Gravity and drag losses: the ideal mass flow
rkt-16-perdas-gravidade.theory:
# The ideal Δv and the Δv that is left

Tsiolkovsky gives the **ideal** Δv: no gravity and no air. In a real flight, part of it is spent just **holding the rocket up against gravity** and **pushing the air aside**:

```
useful Δv ≈ ideal Δv − gravity loss − drag loss
gravity loss ≈ g × burn time   (vertical climb)
```

## Burning slowly: gravity loss

If the engine has a low mass flow, the thrust-to-weight ratio is close to 1 and the burn takes long. Each second of vertical burn "spends" ~9.8 m/s just to avoid falling. A 100 s burn loses ~**981 m/s**!

## Burning fast: drag (and acceleration) loss

With a very high mass flow, the rocket gets very fast while still **in the dense air** down low. Drag ½·ρ·v²·Cd·A grows with the square of the speed, and the acceleration may exceed what the payload and structure can take.

## The middle ground

There is an **optimal** mass flow (or thrust-to-weight), typically T/W of 1.5 to 2.5 for sounding rockets. Orbital launchers lift off at T/W ≈ 1.2–1.5 and **throttle down** near the point of maximum dynamic pressure ("Max Q").

## In this lab

A guided sounding rocket (Isp 230 s, 150 kg of propellant, 50 kg dry mass, 300 mm diameter). The ideal Δv is the same in every try — only **how fast** the propellant burns changes.
rkt-16-perdas-gravidade.task: At 8 kg/s of mass flow the rocket barely passes 36 km and pulls 24 g. Adjust the **mass flow** to pass **130 km** of apogee with a peak acceleration of up to **8 g**.
hints: Lower the mass flow: less drag and fewer g. But watch what happens below 1.5 kg/s.
Watch the thrust-to-weight: the best apogee comes with T/W near 2.

questions.prompt: A rocket climbs vertically burning for **100 s**. What is the approximate gravity loss? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Loss ≈ g × t = 9.81 × 100 = 981 m/s of Δv spent just to avoid falling.

questions.prompt: At 10 km altitude (ρ = **0.38 kg/m³**), the rocket flies at **1000 m/s** with Cd = **0.5** and frontal area **0.07 m²**. What is the drag?
questions.explanation: D = ½ × 0.38 × 1000² × 0.5 × 0.07 = 6650 N — more than the weight of 600 kg!

questions.prompt: With the same amount of propellant, why does a T/W of **1.15** give a poor apogee?
options: Because the ideal Δv becomes smaller
Because the drag is much higher
Because almost all the thrust is spent holding up the weight during a long burn
Because the engine overheats
questions.explanation: The ideal Δv doesn't change (same Isp and masses). With T/W near 1, the net acceleration is small and the gravity loss (g × burn time) is huge.

rkt-17-reentrada.title: Re-entry: coming back from space in one piece
rkt-17-reentrada.theory:
# All the energy has to go

A spacecraft in low orbit flies at ~7.8 km/s. Each kilogram has ½·v² ≈ **30 MJ** of kinetic energy — more than the chemical energy of 7 kg of TNT. To land, almost all of it has to become **heat in the air** in front of the craft.

## Ballistic coefficient

```
β = m / (Cd × A)
```

β tells how "piercing" the object is. **Low β** (light and wide) brakes **high up**, where the air is thin — less, more spread-out heating. **High β** (heavy and slim) dives deep before braking — huge peaks of heat and g. The terminal speed near the ground is:

```
v = √(2 × β × g / ρ)
```

## Blunt bodies

It seems odd, but capsules are **blunt**, not pointed: the flat front creates a **detached shock wave** that stays away from the surface, and much of the heat goes into the air instead of into the craft (H. Julian Allen's idea, 1951).

## Heat shields

- **Ablative** (phenolic resins, PICA): the material chars and flakes off, carrying the heat away. Single use.
- **Reusable** (the Space Shuttle's ceramic tiles, carbon-carbon on the nose and edges): radiate the heat back out.

## The entry corridor

Entering **too steep** produces lethal g and heat; **too shallow**, the craft "skips" off the atmosphere back into space. Crewed capsules keep the deceleration at ~4–8 g by using a little lift (the CG is offset from the axis).

## Finally: parachutes

Below ~10 km, already subsonic, the capsule opens the **drogue** chute and then the **mains**.

questions.prompt: How much kinetic energy does **1 kg** have at **7800 m/s**? Answer in MJ.
A **1000 kg** capsule, **2 m** in diameter, Cd = **1.2**. What is the ballistic coefficient β = m / (Cd × A)?
Without parachutes, what would this capsule's terminal speed be near the ground? (v = √(2βg/ρ), g = 9.81, ρ = 1.225 kg/m³)
questions.explanation: v = √(2 × 265.3 × 9.81 / 1.225) ≈ 65 m/s (~235 km/h): that is why parachutes are essential.

questions.prompt: Why do re-entry capsules have a **blunt** front instead of a pointed one?
options: To fit more people
The shock wave stays detached and away from the surface, and much of the heat stays in the air
Because pointed tips heat up less
To reduce drag
questions.explanation: A pointed body concentrates the heat at the tip; the blunt one pushes the shock away and increases drag, braking higher up.

questions.prompt: What happens if the craft enters the atmosphere at too **shallow** an angle?
options: It heats up much more and breaks apart
It lands farther away, but without trouble
It can "skip" off the atmosphere back into space
The parachutes open too early
questions.explanation: Outside the entry corridor: too steep = lethal g and heat; too shallow = the craft doesn't lose enough speed and leaves the atmosphere.

rkt-18-mecanica-orbital.title: Orbital mechanics: Kepler, escape and geostationary orbit
rkt-18-mecanica-orbital.theory:
# The laws that govern orbits

An orbit is a **free fall that never hits the ground**: the craft is always falling, but moves sideways fast enough for the Earth to "curve away" beneath it.

## Kepler's laws

1. Orbits are **ellipses** with the Earth at one focus.
2. The craft sweeps **equal areas in equal times**: it moves faster at **perigee** (lowest point) and slower at **apogee**.
3. The period depends only on the **semi-major axis** a:

```
T = 2π × √(a³ / GM)
```

With the Earth's GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and radius R = 6371 km, an orbit at 400 km (a = 6771 km) has T ≈ **92 minutes** — the ISS goes around ~15.5 times a day.

## Vis-viva

The speed at any point of the orbit, at distance r from the centre:

```
v = √(GM × (2/r − 1/a))
```

For a circular orbit (r = a): v = √(GM/r). To escape (a → ∞): **v_escape = √(2GM/r)** — from the Earth's surface, ~**11.2 km/s**.

## Geostationary orbit

With a period equal to **one sidereal day** (86 164 s), above the equator, the satellite seems fixed in the sky. By the 3rd law: a = ∛(GM × T² / 4π²) ≈ **42 164 km** from the centre (~35 786 km altitude).

## Hohmann transfer (review)

To go from low orbit to geostationary, the first burn raises the apogee to 42 164 km. The speed at the perigee of the transfer ellipse comes from vis-viva with a = (r1 + r2)/2.

questions.prompt: What is the period of a circular orbit at **400 km** altitude? (GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², R = 6371 km). Answer in minutes.
What is the escape velocity at the Earth's surface? (v = √(2GM/R))
What is the radius of the geostationary orbit (distance from the Earth's centre)? Use T = **86 164 s**.
To leave the **400 km** circular orbit (r1 = 6771 km) for an ellipse with its apogee at geostationary (r2 = 42 164 km), what is the Δv of the first burn? Use vis-viva.
In an elliptical orbit, where does the craft move fastest?
options: At perigee (the point closest to the Earth)
At apogee (the farthest point)
The speed is the same along the whole orbit
It depends on the craft's mass
questions.explanation: Kepler's 2nd law (equal areas in equal times), or vis-viva: smaller r → larger v. The craft's mass doesn't matter.

rkt-19-competicao.title: Competition: exact apogee and flight time
rkt-19-competicao.theory:
# Hit the target, not the highest altitude

In student model rocketry competitions (like the American Rocketry Challenge and its versions in other countries), the challenge is **not** to go as high as possible: it is to reach an **exact altitude** and come back to the ground in an **exact time**, with a fragile payload (an egg) intact. Missing high or low costs points.

## The design levers

- **Motor**: sets the range of possible altitudes (the impulse class).
- **Mass**: the fine tuning of the apogee. Ballast (clay) near the CG changes the altitude without ruining stability.
- **Ejection delay**: should open the parachute **near apogee**, when the speed is lowest (too early tears the chute; too late, the rocket is already falling).
- **Parachute**: sets the **descent speed** and therefore the flight time:

```
flight time ≈ time to apogee + apogee / descent speed
descent speed = √(2 m g / (ρ Cd A))
```

A bigger parachute comes down more slowly (longer flight time, softer landing), but the wind carries the rocket farther.

## Engineering method

In practice, teams make **test flights**, note the altimeter's apogee and correct the mass: each extra gram takes off a few metres. Here you do the same in the simulator.

## In this lab

A 41 mm × 650 mm rocket, ogive nose, 45 mm fins. The dry mass includes the egg and the altimeter.
rkt-19-competicao.task: Contest rules: apogee **between 240 and 260 m**, flight time **between 41 and 46 s**, parachute opening **below 10 m/s** and landing **at up to 7.5 m/s** (the egg must not break). Choose the **motor**, the **dry mass**, the **parachute** and the **delay**.
rkt-19-competicao.safety:
- Model rocketry competitions follow the organiser's **safety code**: certified motors, rocket inspection before flight, a range safety officer in charge.
- If the payload is a **raw egg**, it goes inside padded protection — and the rocket must come back under a parachute, never in free fall.
- Nobody approaches a motor that **misfired** for 60 s.
hints: With the D12, only a very light rocket (under 150 g) reaches 240 m. Try the E9 and adjust the mass 5 g at a time.
Choose the delay so the parachute opens near apogee (apogee time − burn time). Then size the parachute to hit the flight time.
goals: Parachute opens at up to 10 m/s

questions.prompt: A rocket comes down from **250 m** at a constant **6 m/s** under its parachute. How long does the descent take?
The rocket reaches its **240 m** apogee at **8 s** and comes down at **7 m/s**. What is the approximate flight time?
The rocket overshot the target by 20 m. What is the simplest fix, without touching the motor or the parachute?
options: Increase the ejection delay
Add a few grams of ballast near the CG
Remove the fins
Launch with the rod tilted more
questions.explanation: Extra mass lowers the apogee predictably. Near the CG, it barely changes the stability margin.

rkt-20-lancador-orbital.title: Final project: a small orbital launcher
rkt-20-lancador-orbital.theory:
# Putting it all together

An orbital launcher is a compromise between every lesson of this track:

- **Δv**: ~9.4 km/s for low orbit (7.8 km/s of orbital speed + gravity, drag and steering losses). It comes from Tsiolkovsky, stage by stage.
- **Liftoff thrust-to-weight**: at least ~1.3. Below that, gravity loss eats the Δv (and with T/W < 1 the rocket doesn't even leave the pad).
- **Peak acceleration**: at the end of the burn the rocket is light and the acceleration soars. Payloads and crews limit it to ~4–6 g; real engines **throttle down** at the end.
- **Liftoff mass**: it costs money. Each kilogram of payload in orbit takes tens of kilograms on the pad.

## Splitting between stages

The first stage needs **a lot of thrust** (high mass flow) to lift the weight of everything. The second stage is light: it can have a **lower mass flow** (fewer g at the end) and a **higher Isp** (vacuum nozzle). Putting more propellant in the second stage gives more Δv per kilogram — until the first stage can no longer lift the stack.

## In this lab

- Payload + second-stage structure: **1500 kg** (dry mass).
- First-stage structure: **4000 kg** (dropped at separation).
- Isp: **280 s** (first stage, sea level) and **330 s** (second, vacuum nozzle).
- Flight guided by thrust vectoring; the simulator flies vertically, so look at the **ideal Δv**, the **T/W** and the **acceleration** — the apogee is not the goal here.
rkt-20-lancador-orbital.task: Design both stages: **ideal Δv of at least 9400 m/s**, **thrust-to-weight of at least 1.3** at liftoff, peak acceleration of **up to 6 g** and liftoff mass of **up to 56 t**. You control the propellant and the mass flow of each stage.
hints: First move propellant from the 1st to the 2nd stage (keeping the total mass) and watch the Δv rise.
Then raise the 1st-stage mass flow until T/W passes 1.3, and lower the 2nd-stage one if the acceleration exceeds 6 g.
goals: Ideal Δv of at least 9400 m/s

questions.prompt: A first stage with **Isp 300 s** goes from **50 t** to **20 t** during its burn. What is its ideal Δv? (g0 = 9.80665 m/s²)
A **53.5 t** rocket lifts off with **250 kg/s** of mass flow and **Isp 280 s**. What is its thrust-to-weight? (g0 = 9.80665 m/s²)
Why does the peak acceleration usually happen at the **end** of the second-stage burn?
options: Because the engine raises its thrust by itself
Because the air helps to push
Because the thrust is almost constant and the mass has become much smaller
Because gravity vanishes in space
questions.explanation: a = F/m: with the tank almost empty, the same force accelerates a much smaller mass. That's why real engines throttle down at the end.
